When we describe someone or something as solipsistic, we mean they operate as if their own mind, perspective, and experience are the only things that are truly real — and that the inner lives, feelings, and realities of other people barely register, or don't fully compute.

A solipsistic person isn't just self-absorbed in the casual, everyday sense. It goes deeper than that. On some level, they can't — or don't — genuinely process that other people have inner worlds that are just as vivid, valid, and real as their own.

The word comes from a philosophical idea called solipsism, which asks a radical question: "How do I know that anything outside my own mind actually exists?" The strict philosophical answer is: you can't prove it. You can only be certain that your own mind exists — everything else (the world, other people, their feelings) could theoretically be a projection of your imagination.

Now, almost nobody literally believes this in daily life. But when we call someone solipsistic, we're saying they behave as if this were true — as if their own experience is the master copy of reality, and everything else is secondary.
What It Actually Looks Like in Real Life

Here are some concrete pictures to make this click:

Example 1 — The Solipsistic Friend
Imagine a friend who calls you only to talk about themselves. When you share something difficult you're going through, they nod for a second and then redirect the conversation back to their own life. This isn't cruelty — they just genuinely don't process your experience as something real and weighty. Your inner world doesn't fully land for them, because their own is the only one that feels completely real.

Example 2 — The Solipsistic Leader
A politician who dismisses all criticism, contrary evidence, or opposing views — not because they're lying or strategically spinning, but because they genuinely cannot conceive that another person's take on reality might be valid. Their perception of events is reality, in their mind.

Example 3 — The Solipsistic Writer
A writer who produces work so wrapped up in their own private references, feelings, and assumptions that it makes no effort to reach the reader. It reads like a diary written for no audience — because on some level, no audience truly existed in the writer's mind while writing it.

Example 4 — The Solipsistic Child
A young child who thinks everyone at a party is staring at them — not out of vanity, but because in their developing mind, they genuinely are the center of the universe. Young children are naturally solipsistic to a degree; growing up partly means outgrowing this.
The Most Important Distinction: Solipsistic vs. Narcissistic

These two words are very commonly confused. Understanding the difference sharpens your grasp of both.

A narcissist knows other people exist and have inner lives — but believes they are superior to those people and craves their admiration and attention. Their self-obsession is competitive and outward-facing.

A solipsistic person goes a level deeper. It's not about being better than others. It's that other people's inner lives don't feel fully real to them. The solipsistic person isn't competing for the spotlight — they just genuinely experience themselves as the protagonist, and everyone else as background.

A helpful analogy:

  • A narcissist walks into a room and thinks: "Everyone here must be watching me, because I'm extraordinary."
  • A solipsistic person walks into a room and thinks: "I am the main character of this story. Everyone else is a supporting role in my experience of life."

Selfishness is about wanting things for yourself, often at others' expense. You can be selfish and still fully acknowledge that other people have feelings that matter — you just choose to prioritize your own.

Being solipsistic is more foundational. It isn't really about wanting. It's about perceiving. A solipsistic person may not even intend to ignore others — they simply can't fully access the reality that others' inner experiences are as vivid and valid as their own.

Selfishness is a moral failing. Solipsism is more of a perceptual or cognitive one.

In real-world usage, "solipsistic" is almost never used to describe someone who literally believes they are the only conscious being alive. Instead, it describes people who function as if that were true, to varying degrees.

You might say someone is mildly solipsistic — meaning they simply have a hard time taking other people's perspectives seriously and always tend to center themselves in every situation.

Or you might say something is deeply solipsistic — like a memoir so self-referential that it assumes every reader has lived the exact same life as the author.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "His solipsistic worldview made it impossible for him to understand why his employees were frustrated — to him, their concerns simply didn't feel real."
  • "The novel was criticized for being solipsistic — its narrator treated every other character as though they existed only in relation to him."
  • "There's something solipsistic about the way she processes arguments — she can only ever see her own side as legitimate."
  • "Growing up means gradually becoming less solipsistic — learning to genuinely feel that other people's experiences matter as much as your own."
A Summary You Can Carry With You

Solipsistic = treating your own mind, experience, and perspective as the center and measure of reality, in a way that prevents you from fully recognizing or valuing the inner lives of others.

It's deeper than selfishness. It's more subtle than narcissism. It's a mode of being in which the world is experienced almost entirely through one lens — your own — and other people's realities never quite achieve the same weight and realness as your own does.
